chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: Bill Watrous and Jackson's reputation as super sideman
summary: Jackson praises Bill Watrous, who calls him father and practices hours daily; Hinton says trombonists credit Jackson's influence.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: And we got another young trombone player that's coming up today, to me, that is right -- he's right on the verge, and that's Bill Watrous.
That's what he calls me, father.
Because we work together so much, you know.
I think he's a lovable young man and has such potential. His powers -- I don't think he even knows his own strength, as we say.
Well, you know, the kidsshould take
after him. You know, Bill Watrous practices five and six hours every day, legitimately. That's what the kids should learn to do instead of learning to play a solo, you see.
And that's the reason that he produces like he does, and he's doing a lot of clinics around the country now, too, and I hope he is selling the kids.
Of course, the last time I talked to him he told me he was trying. And he tries to tell me about kids talking about me, that kids -- that I had been with Thad Jones, I played clinics.
Well, he was the one that would go around and tell them about you, --

-- that you are truly without a doubt the super sideman. Here's a man, Quentin Jackson, that in all the annals of his history, 50 or 60 years in jazz, that never had a band but has -- excuse me -- helped make so many great bands greater because of your presence with the band. And being highly respected. The reason I'm saying this is because all of these trombone players mentioned to me you and about how you influenced them. J. J. Johnson.
